title: Side Project Graveyard
tagline: Every repo deserves a proper burial.

children.text: Every developer keeps a folder of projects that quietly stopped. This is where mine are laid to rest, each with a stone, a cause of death, and the last commit message it left behind.
Walk slowly. Read a few epitaphs. If one of them looks like something in your own folder, light a candle. It will not bring the project back, but the keeper will notice.

footerLine: Built for the DEV × Sanity Challenge. Nothing here is alive.

title: Lost interest
description: The commits got further apart until one of them turned out to be the last.

title: Scope creep
description: It was going to do one thing, then it was going to do everything, and in the end it did neither.

title: A better tool shipped
description: Someone with a team and a budget released the same idea on an ordinary Tuesday morning.

title: Got a real job
description: The evenings it lived in were given to someone who pays for them.

title: Dependency hell
description: A package three levels down changed its mind, and nothing above it ever installed again.

title: Shipped v1, never looked back
description: It did what it was built to do, went out the door once, and was left in peace.

title: Nobody came
description: It was launched to an audience that turned out to be its author and one bot.

title: Rewrote it in a new framework and never finished
description: The old version worked; the new one was going to be clean, and it is still going to be.

name: Lantern CMS
epitaph: Still serves one dentist's website. Nobody remembers the admin password.

children.text: Lantern was a content management system written in PHP in the spring of 2011, when writing your own content management system was still considered a reasonable weekend.
It grew a template language, a plugin folder, and a user table with one row. By 2014 every client it was built for had moved to a hosted page builder, and the commits thinned to one a season.
The last one is dated 2 February 2015. One installation is still running on a shared host. It belongs to a dentist, and it has not been updated since.

lesson: Software outlives the interest of whoever wrote it. Write the admin password down before the interest goes.

name: One More List
epitaph: It had three tasks. All three were about finishing it.

children.text: One More List was a todo app. It was started on the second day of January 2016, which is when todo apps are started.
It could add a task and cross one out. Deleting a task was planned. The repository holds a single commit, and the app was last opened two days later, to check that it still ran.

lesson: A todo app is a tutorial, not a product. I already owned a notebook.

name: Everything.js
epitaph: It had a router, an ORM and a philosophy. It never had a user.

children.text: Everything.js set out to be the last web framework its author would ever need. It began as forty lines that wrapped an HTTP server.

Then it needed a router. The router needed dependency injection, the injection needed decorators, and the decorators needed a build step, which the framework also provided. A documentation site was started before version 0.1.
No application was ever built on it. The final commit, on 21 June 2019, renamed the core package for the fourth time.

lesson: A framework extracted from zero applications solves zero problems. Build the application first, twice.

name: Nine Tokens
epitaph: Tracked nine tokens in real time. Outlived seven of them.

children.text: Nine Tokens was a dashboard for a wallet with nine tokens in it. It drew a line chart for each, refreshed every ten seconds, and had a dark mode before it had a second page.
It was shared in two group chats in November 2021. Analytics recorded eleven visits that month, nine of them from the same laptop.
By June 2022 seven of the nine charts were flat lines along the bottom of the screen. The prices endpoint was updated one last time on the 14th, and the tab was closed.

lesson: Check that the thing being charted will still exist by the time the chart is finished.

name: Sunday Letter
epitaph: One subscriber, who was me. Open rate: 100%.

children.text: Sunday Letter was a newsletter tool for people who found the existing newsletter tools too large. It sent one plain-text email a week and had no tracking pixels, on principle.
It sent sixteen issues between February and May 2019. Every one was delivered and every one was opened, by the same address.
The last feature added was the unsubscribe link. It was tested once, and it worked.

lesson: Find the second subscriber before building the unsubscribe flow.

name: Quiet Tabs
epitaph: Worked in every version of Chrome but the next one.
lastCommit: bump manifest_version to 3, see what breaks

children.text: Quiet Tabs was a Chrome extension that put idle tabs to sleep after twenty minutes. It had 212 users, most of whom never opened its settings.
It depended on a background page that stayed awake. The new extension manifest did not allow background pages to stay awake. The migration guide was read several times.
On 3 June 2024 the manifest version was changed from 2 to 3 to see what would break. Everything did. The store listing was later taken down by the store, not by the author.

lesson: If a platform can remove me with a blog post, keep the logic that matters out of the platform's API.

name: Pocket Ledger
epitaph: Not dead. Resting. The rewrite has almost caught up with 2022.

children.text: Pocket Ledger is a personal budget app, and the keeper has been asked not to use the past tense. The first version worked. It was written in Vue and tracked groceries for five months.
The second version was going to be cleaner. It is about two thirds of the way to doing what the first one did, and has been since the autumn of 2023.
There is no date on this stone. The author visits every few months, opens the editor, reads the settings page, and closes the editor.

lesson: A rewrite is a second project that inherits the first one's deadline and none of its users.

name: Night Porter
epitaph: Watched four servers until its author was hired to watch four hundred.

children.text: Night Porter was an uptime monitor. Every sixty seconds it asked four servers whether they were still there and wrote the answer to a table.
It was written over one summer between jobs, and it was the main exhibit in three interviews. The third interview went well.
The first day at the new job was 17 August 2015. Alerts were never built, so when Night Porter itself went down, nothing noticed.

lesson: The side project got me the job that ended the side project. I count that as shipped.

name: Inkwell
epitaph: Three posts. 1,412 dependencies. The posts were about the dependencies.

children.text: Inkwell was a static blog generator, built because the existing ones had too many moving parts. It shipped with 1,412 packages in its lockfile.
It published three posts in fifteen months. Each explained how the blog had been built. Between posts, the build broke four times without a single line of its own code changing.
The final commit ran an automated fix with the force flag on 20 January 2020. The build has not passed since.

lesson: Count the dependencies, then count the posts. If the first number is bigger, write in a text file.

name: Umbrella
epitaph: Told me whether it was raining. I had a window.

children.text: Umbrella was a command-line program that printed the weather for one city. It was written in Go over a long weekend in April 2020, when nobody was going outside anyway.
It gained colour output on day three and a JSON flag on day nine. Nothing ever consumed the JSON.

lesson: Solve a problem I actually have. I did not have this one.

name: Fretwork
epitaph: Transposed every song I knew, which was four.

children.text: Fretwork stored guitar chord charts and could move a song into any key. It was started in July 2013, a month after its author bought a guitar.
The transposing worked. The capo calculation was wrong by one fret for most of its life and was corrected in the final commit, on 9 March 2014.
The database holds four songs. The guitar is still in the room, in its case.

lesson: The interest was in the guitar, not the app. The app was a way of not practising.

name: Marginalia
epitaph: Rewritten in three frameworks. Tracked the same eleven books each time.

children.text: Marginalia was a reading tracker: a list of books, a page count, a place for notes. The first version was finished in a month and worked.
It was then rebuilt in a second framework, for the component model, and in a third, for the routing. Each time the same eleven books were migrated by hand.
The fourth start is dated 13 November 2022 and contains a folder structure. No twelfth book was ever added.

lesson: Each rewrite felt like progress and shipped nothing. The eleven books did not care what rendered them.

name: Attic
epitaph: A place for all my notes. It holds two, both about how to organise notes.
lastCommit: add plugin system for future plugins

children.text: Attic was a personal wiki. It was meant to hold everything its author knew, linked in both directions.
In thirteen months it acquired tags, backlinks, a graph view, full-text search, and a plugin system. It did not acquire notes. The database has two entries, and both describe the folder structure.
The plugin system was merged on 19 December 2021. There are no plugins.

lesson: A plugin system with no plugins is a second unfinished app. Write the notes first.

name: Kindness Chain
epitaph: One sentence from you. One dime from me. Verified on-chain.
lastCommit: Pace the chain walk so the public node does not rate-limit it

children.text: Kindness Chain let anyone add one sentence about a kind thing they did or would do that day, with no signup and no wallet. Each sentence became a memo transaction on Solana devnet that carried the signature of the link before it.
It was built in Go for the DEV Weekend Challenge: Generosity Edition, September 4 to 7, 2026. For every confirmed link its author pledged $0.10 to the International Institute of Minnesota, up to $50.
The pledge was settled on 14 September 2026, at 21 links and $2.10. The repository was last pushed that day.

lesson: SQLite is the source of truth and Solana is the public proof. Nothing about a link is invented by the chain writer.

name: GOOD DOG
epitaph: A game where you are the dog. The dog is real.
lastCommit: fixed radio audio on ios by priming speakers inside the tap

children.text: GOOD DOG is a game in which the player spends three days in a shelter as a real dog, one of twelve taken from real shelter listings. The player cannot speak, only bark, whine, growl or stay quiet.
It is a single Go binary with the frontend embedded. The repository was created on 14 August 2026 and last pushed two days later.
One of the twelve dogs, Bella, went home on August 15 while the game was being built, and the game says so.

lesson: The engine owns truth and the model owns wording. A model never decides what happens next.

name: Still Warm
epitaph: A museum where comfort food is the art.

children.text: Still Warm is a museum where comfort food is the art: four rooms of dishes that taste like home, each with a label, and a desk where a visitor can leave a memory that becomes the last exhibit.
It was built with React and TypeScript for the DEV Frontend Challenge: Comfort Food Edition. The keyboard route passes through every room in 27 stops.
The repository was created on 6 August 2026 and last pushed on 12 August 2026. Printing the page produces a catalogue of seven sheets.

lesson: Read contrast from painted pixels, not from tokens. A shadow once took a label to 3.9:1 while axe and Lighthouse both passed it.

name: LinkedIn Radar
epitaph: A daily robot that read the developer internet and threw away the noise.

children.text: LinkedIn Radar scanned Hacker News, GitHub, dev.to, Reddit, release feeds and conference listings every morning, removed the clutter, and turned what was left into a short list of post ideas.
The collectors are small Go programs that use only the standard library. Scoring is a separate stage that runs after them.
The repository was created on 16 June 2026 and last pushed on 3 July 2026.

lesson: Collecting is mechanical and judgement is centralized. Keep the two halves strictly separate.

name: PDF Viewer SDK
epitaph: A client-side PDF viewer SDK. Created and last pushed on the same day.

children.text: PDF Viewer SDK was a take-home assignment: a client-side PDF viewer SDK built with Vite, React and TypeScript.
The repository has three folders. A holds the application, B holds the architecture and design document, and C holds the Cursor AI usage log. GitHub lists its primary language as HTML.
It was created on 7 April 2026 and last pushed the same day.

lesson: Keep the architecture document and the usage log next to the code, each in its own folder.
